title: The Ethics Tribunal
theme: HR Ethics, Organizational Justice, and the Weight of Hard Calls
description: You are the Chief People Officer of a 400-person company. Five cases have landed on your desk — each one genuinely difficult, each one watched by the organization more carefully than you might think. For each case you will review the facts, make a decision, and then — six months later — see what actually happened. There is no answer key. Every choice you make has real costs and real benefits. The game does not reward the 'right' answer because in HR ethics, the right answer often depends on values you have to choose between. It rewards thinking carefully about what you're actually optimizing for.
learning_concept: Organizational culture is not built from stated values — it is built from how edge cases are handled. Every difficult HR decision is a cultural signal that spreads through the organization whether you intend it to or not.
learning_objectives: Understand the difference between rules-based justice (applying policy consistently) and values-based justice (asking what outcome serves the organization's actual principles)
Recognize the systemic effects of individual HR decisions — how other employees read and interpret what happens to someone else
Practice holding two legitimate values in tension without collapsing into easy resolution: fairness to individuals versus fairness to the organization, accountability versus rehabilitation
Build tolerance for the discomfort of decisions that have no clean answer — and develop the skill of making the best available choice while naming its costs

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: You are the CPO (Chief People Officer) — five difficult HR cases have come to you over the course of one year
Each case is presented across two rounds: Round A presents the facts and asks for your HR decision; Round B reveals what actually happened six months later as a result of your choice
For each decision, choose from three options ranging from more lenient to more strict — but be aware that both extremes carry costs
Track Organizational Trust, Fairness Perception, and Policy Strength as they shift with each decision — these affect how the organization reads your future choices
There is no correct answer. The game surfaces the costs of every option. Your goal is to make the best decision you can with the information available, and sit with what it costs.
tips: Other employees are always watching — your decision about one person sends a message to everyone else about what kind of organization this is
Leniency and strictness are both legitimate tools. The question is whether you're applying them based on your values or your discomfort
Organizational Trust and Fairness Perception can move in opposite directions — decisions that feel procedurally fair may feel interpersonally punitive, and vice versa
The six-month consequence round is not a judgment of your decision — it is a realistic view of downstream effects. Sometimes good decisions have bad outcomes and vice versa
Ask yourself before each choice: who benefits from this decision, who is harmed, and who is watching?

psychological_framework.description: Organizational justice research (Greenberg, 1987; Folger & Cropanzano, 1998) identifies three distinct forms of fairness that employees monitor: distributive justice (did they get what they deserved?), procedural justice (was the process fair?), and interactional justice (were they treated with dignity?). The most credible HR decisions score well on all three — but these can conflict. Additionally, research by Amy Edmondson on psychological safety shows that how organizations handle edge cases is the primary driver of whether employees believe it is safe to raise concerns, make mistakes, and be honest. Every case in this game is an edge case.

core_skills.name: Empathy
core_skills.description: The capacity to hold the perspective of multiple people simultaneously — the person under review, the people affected by their behavior, and the silent majority watching how this is handled

core_skills.name: Delayed Gratification
core_skills.description: The ability to make decisions based on long-term organizational health rather than what resolves the immediate discomfort — especially when the long-term right thing is harder in the short term

core_skills.name: Strategic Thinking
core_skills.description: Understanding the systemic effects of individual decisions — how what you do in one case shapes the implicit contract of the entire organization

core_skills.name: Resilience
core_skills.description: The capacity to make difficult decisions without knowing the outcome, to hold their costs without either rationalizing them away or being paralyzed by them

glossary_terms.definition: Distributive justice asks whether the outcome was fair; procedural justice asks whether the process was fair. Employees often accept difficult outcomes if they believe the process was fair — and reject favorable outcomes if they believe the process was arbitrary
glossary_terms.example: An employee who is put on a performance improvement plan may accept it if they were given clear warning and objective criteria. The same employee may reject a promotion given without clear criteria, even if they were the right choice.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Research shows that procedural fairness (transparent, consistent, well-documented processes) is the single strongest predictor of employee acceptance of negative decisions. Organizations that invest in procedural clarity have dramatically lower legal challenges, lower resentment, and higher trust — even when decisions go against individuals.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Amazon's Leadership Principles explicitly distinguish between 'have backbone, disagree and commit' and arbitrary authority — the procedural framework matters as much as the outcome. Organizations with clear behavioral frameworks for difficult decisions tend to have lower perceived arbitrariness even in hard cases.

glossary_terms.term: The Signal Function of Edge Cases
glossary_terms.definition: In organizational culture, how leadership handles unusual or difficult cases sends a clearer signal about actual values than stated policies or culture documents
glossary_terms.example: If a top performer is allowed to behave in ways that would terminate a lower performer, the actual organizational value (as opposed to the stated one) is that results protect behavior — regardless of what the handbook says
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Edgar Schein's model of organizational culture distinguishes between artifacts (what you say), espoused values (what you claim to believe), and basic underlying assumptions (what you actually do under pressure). Edge case handling is where basic underlying assumptions become visible to everyone. Organizations consistently surprise researchers by how accurately employees can predict what will happen in an edge case before it happens.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Uber's 2017 culture crisis began not with a single incident but with years of edge cases that were handled in ways that signaled certain behaviors were protected. Susan Fowler's account was remarkable not because the incidents were unique but because she documented how predictably the organization's response pattern replicated itself.

glossary_terms.definition: The organizational tension between treating a policy violation as correctable behavior (investing in change) versus treating it as revealing information about character (changing who you employ)
glossary_terms.example: An employee who harassed a colleague and shows genuine remorse may be a rehabilitation candidate. The same employee in a management role, with three prior HR conversations, presents a different accountability calculus.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Research on workplace rehabilitation suggests that genuine behavior change following HR intervention is possible but requires three conditions: the individual acknowledges the impact of their behavior (not just their intent), they understand why it was wrong rather than just that it was against policy, and there is a concrete behavioral change plan with accountability. Absent these three conditions, rehabilitation almost never occurs.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Google's 2018 employee walkout was triggered partly by the revelation that senior executives who had settled harassment cases had been allowed to resign quietly with large severance packages — a decision that was framed internally as avoiding public disruption but was received by employees as valuing leadership continuity over accountability.

halftime_config.reflection_question: Looking at the decisions you've made in Cases 1 and 2 — what value have you been most consistently trying to protect? And what value have you been most willing to sacrifice when they conflict?
halftime_config.custom_message: You're halfway through five cases. The second half tends to be harder — the cases are messier, the power dynamics more complex, and the downstream consequences more ambiguous. The organization is watching all of it.

rounds.title: Case 1A: The Credit Thief (Decision)
rounds.story: Priya is a senior manager, five years at the company, well-regarded in leadership circles. Over the past six months, three different junior team members have come to you separately with variations of the same complaint: Priya presents their work as her own in senior meetings, rarely credits individuals by name, and when asked about specific work products in meetings, lets the credit accumulate to her without correcting the record. None of the three complainants want to file a formal complaint — they say the culture makes that feel too risky. They came to you informally. Priya's last performance review scored her as 'exceeds expectations.' Her manager — a VP — considers her one of his best people. There is no formal documentation of this behavior in her file.
rounds.goal: Decide how to respond to an informal pattern of credit-taking by a senior manager — with no formal complaint, no documentation, and a strong performance record.
rounds.coaching_moment: This case tests the difference between procedural fairness (you have no formal complaint to act on) and values-based action (three people told you something important informally). Both matter. The question is which one you weight more heavily and what that signals.

choices.label: Have a direct developmental conversation with Priya — name the pattern specifically and make it a coaching conversation, not a disciplinary one
choices.feedback: You schedule time with Priya and tell her directly: 'I've heard from three team members, informally, that they feel their work isn't being credited in senior settings. I'm not here to take action on this — I'm here to name it, because I think you may not be aware of the impact.' Priya is defensive initially, then quiet. She says she hadn't seen it that way. You don't know if that's true. You set a follow-up in 60 days. The junior team members, whose names you protected, don't know what happened. They're still watching. The conversation may change behavior — or it may not. The cost of this approach is that it relies on Priya's willingness to change without accountability. The benefit is it doesn't trigger the formal machinery before the informal one has been tried.
choices.coaching_moment: Informal developmental conversations are legitimate first responses — but only if they include clear articulation of the behavior's impact and a genuine follow-up. Without those, they read as protection of the senior employee rather than genuine development.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You schedule time with Priya and tell her directly: 'I've heard from three team members, informally, that they feel their work isn't being credited in senior settings. I'm not here to take action on this — I'm here to name it, because I think you may not be aware of the impact.

choices.label: Create formal documentation in Priya's file and require her manager to have a structured conversation with specific expectations going forward
choices.feedback: You escalate to Priya's VP manager and require a structured conversation documented in Priya's file, with behavioral expectations about attribution practices going forward. Priya finds out quickly that three informal complaints triggered formal documentation — and that her informal conversations with you were not actually informal. Her trust in HR drops significantly. Her manager is frustrated that you went above him without involving him first. The three junior employees feel vindicated but also worried about retaliation. Policy strength goes up. The relationship cost is real. You've created clear accountability — at the price of the signal that 'informal conversations with HR are actually formal' going forward.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You escalate to Priya's VP manager and require a structured conversation documented in Priya's file, with behavioral expectations about attribution practices going forward. Priya finds out quickly that three informal complaints triggered formal documentation — and that her informal conversations with you were not actually informal.

choices.label: Do nothing formally, but build a systemic attribution practice — require all managers to name individual contributors in senior presentations
choices.feedback: You don't address Priya directly at all. Instead, you bring a new practice to the leadership team: 'Going forward, all senior presentations should name the individuals whose work is being presented. Here's how this will work.' It's a systemic response to a pattern that may extend beyond Priya. The three junior employees, when they see the new practice, don't know if their complaints caused it — they just see it happen. Priya, specifically, is now required to credit her team by name. The behavior changes through structure rather than confrontation. The cost: Priya is not held accountable for the six months of past behavior, and the three junior employees never receive a clear signal that what happened to them was named and taken seriously.

rounds.reflection_prompt: What social or organisational pressures make it tempting to claim credit that isn't fully yours?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

dissent_juror.dissent_reason: the systemic attribution fix prevents the next Priya — punishing one person leaves the structural pattern intact
dissent_juror.juror_persona: Justice Anjali Rao, a senior contrarian juror — soft-spoken but unwilling to let the panel rationalise away harm. She leads with the second-order consequence the majority is willing to absorb.
juror_persona_ladder: a senior contrarian juror who refuses to let the panel rationalise the easier verdict — soft-spoken, names the harm directly
a sharper version of the same juror — quoting the player's own justification back at them and pressing on the second-order consequence the player skipped
a former victim of an analogous decision sitting in the gallery — speaking from the cost of being on the receiving end of the player's reasoning, still 1–2 sentences and a question

rounds.title: Case 1B: Six Months Later — The Credit Thief Consequence
rounds.story: Six months have passed since your Case 1 decision. Here is what happened: One of the three junior employees who came to you informally — Rishi, a particularly talented product analyst — has accepted an offer from a competitor. In his exit interview, he named the credit-taking pattern as a significant factor. He also mentioned that he came to you with the concern and 'nothing seemed to change.' Two of the other junior employees remain at the company but have become visibly less collaborative in cross-functional settings. And Priya is still performing well by the metrics her manager tracks — the VPs still consider her excellent. The pattern may or may not have changed. No one is sure.
rounds.goal: Absorb the downstream consequences of your Case 1 decision and understand what they tell you about the costs of each approach.
rounds.coaching_moment: Rishi's departure is not a verdict on whether your decision was wrong. Every option had costs. But his exit interview framing — 'nothing seemed to change' — reveals something important about the gap between what you did and what he perceived. The perception gap is its own organizational problem.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Rishi said 'nothing seemed to change.' Whatever you chose in Case 1 — what did you do to make sure the people who raised the concern understood that something was being done? If you didn't close that loop, why not?

choices.label: Reach out to the remaining two employees and be explicit: 'I heard your concern. Here's what changed and what didn't. I want to hear how it's been for you.'
choices.feedback: You reach out to both remaining employees directly and have individual conversations. You don't disclose what happened with Priya specifically, but you acknowledge their concern, tell them that action was taken at the level you could take it, and ask how things have felt since. One of them — Anya — says it's slightly better but she still doesn't trust the culture enough to raise concerns again. The other, Vikram, is still skeptical but appreciates the follow-up. Neither is planning to leave. The conversations don't fix everything — but they close the perception gap that cost you Rishi. Organizations that lose trust usually lose it not from the original decision but from the silence that follows.

choices.label: Use Rishi's exit interview to build a case for a broader culture audit — make this a systemic conversation at the leadership level
choices.feedback: You take Rishi's exit interview — anonymized — to the leadership team and present it as evidence of a systemic culture concern: not specifically about Priya, but about whether junior employees feel their work is recognized and whether they feel safe raising concerns about senior managers. The VP who manages Priya is uncomfortable. The CEO asks what you recommend. You propose a structured listening program — skip-level conversations quarterly across all of product and engineering. It's a credible, scaled response. It doesn't address the two remaining employees individually, and it won't reach Rishi who is already gone. But it turns one departure into organizational learning.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You take Rishi's exit interview — anonymized — to the leadership team and present it as evidence of a systemic culture concern: not specifically about Priya, but about whether junior employees feel their work is recognized and whether they feel safe raising concerns about senior managers. The VP who manages Priya is uncomfortable.

choices.label: Accept the outcome and use it to revise your policy on how informal HR concerns are handled and closed
choices.feedback: Rishi's departure clarifies something for you: your current policy has no formal protocol for closing the loop with employees who raise informal concerns. You revise this — going forward, any informal HR concern that triggers an action will include a confidential follow-up with the person who raised it within 60 days. Not disclosing what happened — but confirming that something happened. The policy change is sound and probably prevents future Rishis. It doesn't help Rishi, or the two remaining employees whose trust is already partially eroded. Systemic fixes are necessary. They are also insufficient replacements for the individual human moment you didn't take.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Rishi's departure clarifies something for you: your current policy has no formal protocol for closing the loop with employees who raise informal concerns. You revise this — going forward, any informal HR concern that triggers an action will include a confidential follow-up with the person who raised it within 60 days.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Case 2A: The Racist Joke (Decision)
rounds.story: Devansh works in the customer success team. He's been with the company three years and his performance scores are solid — not exceptional, not problematic. At a team offsite last week, he made a comment about a colleague from a different ethnic background. The comment was, in Devansh's word, 'a joke' — he says he meant it affectionately. The colleague, Arun, was visibly uncomfortable but did not respond in the moment. Three others in the room heard it. One of them filed a formal HR complaint two days later. Arun has not filed a complaint and says he does not want to escalate — he says it was uncomfortable but he doesn't want to make it a bigger thing. You've interviewed all five people in the room. The accounts are consistent. Devansh says he understands the comment was received badly and expresses genuine-seeming remorse.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle a confirmed incident of a racially insensitive comment where the person targeted does not want to escalate and the person who made it shows apparent remorse.
rounds.coaching_moment: This case forces a tension between respecting Arun's stated wish not to escalate and the obligation to address an incident that multiple people witnessed and one person formally reported. Arun's preference is real. It is also not the only consideration.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Arun said he does not want to make this a bigger thing. How much weight should his stated preference carry in your decision? What are the costs of following it exactly, and what are the costs of overriding it?

choices.label: Issue a formal written warning to Devansh documented in his file, require mandatory anti-bias training, and notify the team that the incident was addressed formally
choices.feedback: You issue Devansh a formal written warning, place it in his file, and require completion of anti-bias training within 30 days. You notify the team that the incident was formally addressed — not what happened to Devansh, but that the concern raised was taken seriously. Arun is unhappy when he finds out — he specifically said he did not want escalation. He comes to you and says he feels like his preference was ignored. You explain your reasoning: the incident involved others, one person formally reported it, and you have an obligation that isn't contingent on one person's preference. Arun says he understands but that he no longer feels comfortable coming to HR with concerns. The policy signal is strong. The interpersonal trust cost is real.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You issue Devansh a formal written warning, place it in his file, and require completion of anti-bias training within 30 days. You notify the team that the incident was formally addressed — not what happened to Devansh, but that the concern raised was taken seriously.

choices.label: Have a structured conversation with Devansh — make it a serious but non-punitive developmental intervention with no formal documentation
choices.feedback: You choose a developmental response: a structured conversation with Devansh, without formal documentation, where you name exactly what was problematic about the comment and what behavioral change is expected. You follow Arun's stated preference not to escalate. The three witnesses remain aware that something happened. The person who filed the formal complaint follows up two weeks later to ask what the outcome was. When you tell her a 'conversation was had,' she replies: 'That's it?' She doesn't file a formal escalation — but she stops attending optional company events. Two months later she shares in a Glassdoor review that 'HR talks about inclusion but doesn't back it up with action.' The cost of protecting the relationship with Arun and Devansh was paid by the culture.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You choose a developmental response: a structured conversation with Devansh, without formal documentation, where you name exactly what was problematic about the comment and what behavioral change is expected. You follow Arun's stated preference not to escalate.

choices.label: Meet with Arun first before deciding — be transparent that you have an obligation to respond but want to understand his full perspective before determining how
choices.feedback: You meet with Arun again and say: 'I want to be transparent with you. I have an obligation to respond to this incident because others witnessed it and one person formally reported it. That obligation doesn't disappear based on your preference, and I think you'd want to know that before I make my decision. I'm here to hear whether there's anything more you want me to know that would shape how I respond.' Arun sits with it. He says: 'I appreciate you being honest about your constraints. Here's what actually bothered me most about what Devansh said.' The conversation is more substantive than the first one. Your eventual response is a written warning — but Arun, this time, understands why. He doesn't feel overridden. He feels consulted.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

dissent_juror.dissent_reason: going to the harmed party first respects their agency rather than treating them as evidence in a process they didn't ask for
dissent_juror.juror_persona: Justice Anjali Rao, a senior contrarian juror — soft-spoken but unwilling to let the panel rationalise away harm. She leads with the second-order consequence the majority is willing to absorb.

rounds.title: Case 2B: Six Months Later — The Racist Joke Consequence
rounds.story: Six months have passed. Devansh is still at the company — his performance scores remain solid. Arun transferred to a different team three months ago. He said it was for career development reasons; his new manager thinks he's doing well. The person who filed the formal complaint, Lalitha, is still at the company but has had minimal interaction with the HR function since. The team that was at the offsite has had normal turnover — no pattern around the incident specifically. The incident itself is not openly discussed. But you know from informal conversations that it is remembered. Someone mentioned it as a reference point in a diversity and inclusion survey response: 'We say the right things but the test is what happens when someone says the wrong thing.'
rounds.goal: Absorb the six-month consequence and reflect on what the downstream picture tells you about your Case 2 decision.
rounds.coaching_moment: Arun's transfer may be unrelated to the incident. Or it may be the quietest possible form of self-protection — moving away from an environment where something uncomfortable happened and no one can quite tell what it meant. You may never know which.

choices.label: Check in with Lalitha directly — the person who filed the formal complaint has been quiet and you want to understand her current experience
choices.feedback: You reach out to Lalitha and ask if she'd be willing to have a conversation. She agrees. She tells you directly: 'I filed a formal complaint because I thought it mattered. I don't know what happened afterward. That uncertainty — not knowing if anything changed — is the thing that made me stop trusting the process.' You explain, without disclosing Devansh's specific situation, that action was taken at the appropriate level and that your follow-up with her is part of a process change you're implementing. She says: 'Why didn't someone tell me that three months ago?' You don't have a good answer. The conversation improves your relationship with her — but confirms the gap you already knew existed.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You reach out to Lalitha and ask if she'd be willing to have a conversation. She agrees.

choices.label: Use the survey response as a catalyst — present it to leadership and propose that the company define what 'a real response to an incident looks like' as a public commitment
choices.feedback: You bring the survey response to the CEO and the leadership team, anonymized, and propose that the company make an explicit public commitment to how it handles incidents of bias or harassment — not just to policy, but to transparency about process. What happens after a report is filed? What can a reporter expect to know? What is the timeline? This forces a difficult conversation about privacy versus transparency that takes three months to resolve. The outcome is imperfect but real: a published 'what happens when you report' document on the internal intranet. Three months later, the survey response about 'what happens when someone says the wrong thing' is quoted in an all-hands as the specific catalyst for the change. The culture has moved.

choices.label: Investigate whether Arun's transfer was voluntary or a form of quiet exit from the incident — get to the truth before assuming everything is fine
choices.feedback: You reach out to Arun's new manager and to Arun himself. You ask Arun directly: 'I want to check in — not about the incident specifically, but about how you're doing. The transfer happened and I wanted to make sure it was what you wanted.' Arun pauses. Then says: 'It was and it wasn't. I wanted a change. I also felt like staying in that team meant carrying something that no one else seemed to be carrying.' That's not an accusation — it's a description of a real experience. You cannot undo it. But knowing it is real changes what you do next. Choosing not to know the downstream cost of your decisions is a form of managerial comfort-seeking. Knowing it — and sitting with it — is what doing this job well actually requires.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You reach out to Arun's new manager and to Arun himself. You ask Arun directly: 'I want to check in — not about the incident specifically, but about how you're doing.

rounds.reflection_prompt: When you witness an incident but are not the target, what is your responsibility — and what stops people from acting?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Case 3A: The Top Performer's Expense Fraud (Decision)
rounds.story: Meera runs the enterprise sales team. She has been the top performer in the company for three consecutive years. Last quarter she brought in $4.2M in new ARR — more than any other single contributor. Her manager considers her irreplaceable, and the CEO has mentioned her by name in all-hands as an example of what the company's best looks like. A routine expense audit has flagged $3,800 in questionable expense reports over 18 months: meals slightly above policy, a hotel upgrade beyond the approved tier, a client dinner where the guest list appears to have included personal friends. The auditor has flagged it as likely intentional — the pattern suggests awareness of the policy limits. Meera has not yet been informed.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle confirmed evidence of small-scale expense fraud by your highest-performing revenue contributor.
rounds.coaching_moment: The math here is deliberately uncomfortable: $3,800 versus $4.2M in ARR. But if the decision were purely financial, you wouldn't be thinking about it as an ethics question. The question is whether the same behavior from a different employee — say, a junior analyst with average performance — would result in the same response. And if the answer is different, what does that mean?
rounds.reflection_prompt: Before choosing: if the exact same expense pattern had been flagged for a junior employee with average performance reviews, what would you do? Now apply that logic to Meera. If your answer is different — name why. Is the reason defensible?

choices.label: Apply the standard policy: require Meera to repay the $3,800, issue a formal written warning, and document it in her file
choices.feedback: You apply policy uniformly: Meera is informed of the findings, required to repay $3,800, and receives a formal written warning. Her manager is furious. He tells you directly that you're going to lose her. Meera is shocked and defensive — she says the policy was unclear in some of the edge cases. She repays the money within a week and says very little else. Over the next three months, you watch carefully. She stays. Her performance does not decline. In the sales team, word spreads informally: 'Even Meera got written up.' The message — that no one is above policy — is received. It cost you some managerial goodwill. It purchased organizational fairness in a very visible way.

choices.label: Handle it informally — have a private conversation with Meera, require repayment, no formal documentation
choices.feedback: You handle it off the books: you meet with Meera privately, explain what the audit found, require repayment, and ask her to be more careful going forward. No documentation. Meera is relieved and grateful. Her manager is relieved. Six months later, the auditor who flagged the original issue mentions — in a different context — that they had flagged another similar case involving a less senior employee which resulted in a formal written warning. Someone connects the dots. Three people from the enterprise sales team are in a conversation channel where someone asks directly: 'Is it true Meera's expense situation was handled differently?' The message — that the rules apply differently based on how much revenue you bring — is now part of the unofficial organizational record. It will outlast the original incident by years.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You handle it off the books: you meet with Meera privately, explain what the audit found, require repayment, and ask her to be more careful going forward. No documentation.

choices.label: Use this as a catalyst to clarify expense policy ambiguity for everyone before acting on Meera specifically
choices.feedback: You realize the expense policy has genuine grey areas — the auditor's own notes mention that several of the flagged items fall in policy edge cases. You first issue a company-wide policy clarification that makes the grey areas explicit. Then you address Meera's specific situation under the clarified framework. Under the clearer policy, two of the five flagged items are technically within policy; three are not. Meera is required to repay the three that are clearly outside policy ($1,900) and receives a written note in her file rather than a formal warning. Her manager is still unhappy. But the decision now rests on a firmer policy foundation and is harder to characterize as arbitrary. The clarification benefits everyone — but critics note that the timing looks like it was designed to give Meera a softer outcome.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You realize the expense policy has genuine grey areas — the auditor's own notes mention that several of the flagged items fall in policy edge cases. You first issue a company-wide policy clarification that makes the grey areas explicit.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

dissent_juror.dissent_reason: uniform policy application is the only credible signal that performance doesn't buy exemption — the precedent is the message
dissent_juror.juror_persona: Justice Anjali Rao, a senior contrarian juror — soft-spoken but unwilling to let the panel rationalise away harm. She leads with the second-order consequence the majority is willing to absorb.

rounds.title: Case 3B: Six Months Later — The Top Performer Consequence
rounds.story: Six months have passed since the Meera decision. Meera is still the top revenue performer — she hit 140% of her Q2 number. The expense incident is not openly discussed but is known. A new sales hire, Jatin, submitted an expense report this month with several items flagged by the same auditor. Jatin's expense pattern is nearly identical to Meera's flagged items. The auditor has asked HR to review it. Jatin is mid-level, performing at target. Two members of the auditing team are watching closely to see whether the response is the same.
rounds.goal: Handle the downstream consequence of your Meera decision: a nearly identical situation has now arisen with a lower-profile employee.
rounds.coaching_moment: Whatever you did with Meera, you are now going to do with Jatin under conditions where the consistency will be evaluated. Organizations reveal their values not in isolated incidents but in patterns across similar incidents. This is the moment where the pattern becomes visible.

choices.label: Apply exactly the same response you applied to Meera — whatever that was
choices.feedback: You apply the same response to Jatin that you applied to Meera. If you gave Meera a formal warning, Jatin gets a formal warning. If you handled Meera informally, Jatin gets handled informally. Consistency is the only defensible position, and consistency in this moment is visible. The two auditors who were watching share a brief note: 'Same response, consistent application.' Fairness Perception increases significantly — not because the decision is popular, but because it's predictable. Predictability is the foundation of policy-based trust. Whatever the costs of your original decision, you have now made it into a principle rather than an exception.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You apply the same response to Jatin that you applied to Meera. If you gave Meera a formal warning, Jatin gets a formal warning.

choices.label: Apply a stricter response to Jatin — argue that the Meera situation had mitigating context that Jatin's does not
choices.feedback: You argue internally that Meera's situation had context that Jatin's doesn't — she had a longer tenure, a specific ambiguity in the policy she relied on, and a different pattern. Jatin receives a formal warning while Meera's case remains sealed. The auditor who flagged both cases submits a written concern to your manager asking whether the standard is being applied consistently. Within a month, both situations — and the different outcomes — have been discussed in enough channels to reach the legal team, who sends a note to the CEO. The perception that performance protects policy violations is now not just informal gossip but a documented concern.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You argue internally that Meera's situation had context that Jatin's doesn't — she had a longer tenure, a specific ambiguity in the policy she relied on, and a different pattern. Jatin receives a formal warning while Meera's case remains sealed.

choices.label: Use this second incident to formally review and standardize the expense violation response policy for all future cases
choices.feedback: You pause the Jatin response briefly, address it consistently with Meera's outcome, and simultaneously initiate a formal policy standardization: expense violation responses by amount, frequency, and context — documented, consistent, and published to managers. The process takes six weeks. Jatin's case is resolved under the draft framework. When the final framework is published, the auditing team lead sends you a note: 'This is what a policy looks like.' The cost: the six-week delay created some internal tension and the impression of ad-hoc decision-making in a specific case. The benefit: you've now converted a painful pattern into institutional knowledge that will survive you.

rounds.title: Case 4A: The Whistleblower (Decision)
rounds.story: Six weeks ago, a journalist published a detailed investigative piece about potential safety issues in your company's hardware product line. The story was accurate — it cited internal testing data that had not been made public. Legal has traced the source of the leak. It is Farrukh, a senior quality engineer who has worked at the company for six years and has an exemplary performance record. Farrukh did not approach the journalist recklessly — internal records show he had raised the safety concern through three different channels over 14 months, including a formal submission to the product safety committee, before going external. The safety concern itself is being investigated and may have merit. Farrukh has not been informed that he's been identified. Legal is recommending termination for breach of confidentiality and NDA violation. The CEO has not yet weighed in directly.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle an employee who leaked confidential information to the press — but only after exhausting internal channels for a concern that may be legitimate.
rounds.coaching_moment: This case tests the difference between rules and values more sharply than any other. Farrukh violated the NDA — that is not ambiguous. He also raised a safety concern internally three times over 14 months and was not heard. The organization's failure to hear him is not a defense of his leak — but it is morally relevant to how you respond.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Before you decide: what message does each option send to the next person who discovers a safety concern and wonders whether to raise it internally? And does that message reflect the values the company says it holds?

choices.label: Terminate Farrukh for NDA violation — apply the policy cleanly and address the internal escalation failure separately
choices.feedback: You terminate Farrukh's employment for breach of NDA. The policy is clear and you apply it. You simultaneously launch an internal review of how his three escalations were handled and why the safety concern sat unresolved for 14 months. Legal is satisfied. The CEO says nothing publicly. In the next quarter's internal safety submission period, submissions drop by 40%. Three members of the quality engineering team request transfers to other departments. The message received — even though you added the internal review — is this: 'The person who raised a safety concern publicly got fired.' The policy was applied correctly. The cultural cost was severe.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You terminate Farrukh's employment for breach of NDA. The policy is clear and you apply it.

choices.label: Implement a disciplinary response short of termination — a formal warning and a 90-day PIP — while publicly acknowledging the internal escalation failure
choices.feedback: You issue Farrukh a formal written warning for NDA violation — it is documented, serious, and real. You do not terminate. And simultaneously, you have the CEO send an all-hands communication acknowledging that an employee's safety concern was raised internally three times and not resolved, that this was a failure of the organization's escalation process, and that a specific fix is being implemented. The message is uncomfortable for leadership but necessary. Farrukh keeps his job. He becomes, informally, the person who proved that raising safety concerns internally matters — because even when it went wrong, the company eventually heard it. Safety submissions in the next quarter increase.

choices.label: Consult legal on whistleblower protection law before deciding — determine what the actual legal framework allows and constrains
choices.feedback: You ask legal to do a full analysis of Farrukh's situation under applicable whistleblower protection law before making any HR decision. Legal's analysis takes two weeks and reveals significant complexity: depending on jurisdiction and the specific nature of the safety concern, Farrukh may have qualified legal protection under product safety whistleblower provisions. The termination option carries real legal exposure. The outcome: a disciplinary response short of termination, combined with a formal policy review. The process took two weeks and created some tension — leadership wanted a faster decision. But the decision you ultimately make is on much firmer ground than a reactive termination would have been.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You ask legal to do a full analysis of Farrukh's situation under applicable whistleblower protection law before making any HR decision. Legal's analysis takes two weeks and reveals significant complexity: depending on jurisdiction and the specific nature of the safety concern, Farrukh may have qualified legal protection under product safety whistleblower provisions.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

dissent_juror.dissent_reason: consulting legal on whistleblower protection is not a delay tactic — it is the gating question that determines whether anything else is even lawful
dissent_juror.juror_persona: Justice Anjali Rao, a senior contrarian juror — soft-spoken but unwilling to let the panel rationalise away harm. She leads with the second-order consequence the majority is willing to absorb.
juror_persona_ladder: a senior contrarian juror who refuses to let the panel rationalise the easier verdict — soft-spoken, names the harm directly
a sharper version of the same juror — quoting the player's own justification back at them and pressing on the second-order consequence the player skipped
a former victim of an analogous decision sitting in the gallery — speaking from the cost of being on the receiving end of the player's reasoning, still 1–2 sentences and a question

rounds.title: Case 4B: Six Months Later — The Whistleblower Consequence
rounds.story: Six months later: The safety investigation has concluded. The concern Farrukh raised was partially valid — the product team identified a failure mode that had not been adequately tested. A design modification has been implemented. The journalist has written a follow-up piece that describes the company as having 'addressed the concern after public pressure.' The company is considering whether to be more proactive in its public communications about what was fixed. Farrukh is still at the company — or left, depending on what you decided. The quality engineering team's safety submission rate has either recovered or not.
rounds.goal: Determine the most constructive response to the six-month aftermath of the whistleblower case — and what it reveals about what was learned.
rounds.coaching_moment: The safety concern was real. Farrukh was right. The question of whether he was right to go external doesn't change the fact that the organization failed to hear him for 14 months. What you do with that failure — whether you institutionalize the learning or move on — is the real decision.

choices.label: Be proactive with the journalist — offer a direct interview with the head of safety about what was changed and what was learned
choices.feedback: The company reaches out to the journalist proactively and offers direct access to the safety engineering lead to discuss what was found and fixed. The resulting article is more balanced than the original — it describes a company that responded seriously to a real concern. Farrukh is not mentioned by name. But internally, the gesture signals something: the company is more interested in being accurate than in defending its image. The quality engineering team notices. Safety submissions in the next review period are at a five-year high. Transparency about failure, voluntarily offered, is a different kind of organizational trust-builder than transparency under pressure.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: The company reaches out to the journalist proactively and offers direct access to the safety engineering lead to discuss what was found and fixed. The resulting article is more balanced than the original — it describes a company that responded seriously to a real concern.

choices.label: Publish an internal post-mortem on how Farrukh's internal escalations were handled — name the specific failure points in the escalation process
choices.feedback: You publish an internal post-mortem — shared with all employees — that describes, specifically and without naming Farrukh, how the internal escalation process failed: what happened to each of his three submissions, who was responsible at each step, and what has changed. It is uncomfortable reading for several managers. The CEO comments on it in an all-hands: 'This is what accountability looks like from the inside.' Three months later, a different quality engineer raises a product concern through the new escalation path. It is resolved in 18 days. The system worked because you made the failure visible enough that people understood why the fix mattered.

choices.label: Promote Farrukh to lead the new internal safety escalation program — make the person who surfaced the gap the person who fixes it
choices.feedback: You recommend Farrukh for a new role: head of the internal product safety escalation process. This is only possible if he's still at the company — and it's a significant rehabilitation signal regardless of what disciplinary action you took. The CEO approves it. The message in the organization is unmistakable: the person who found a real problem, raised it repeatedly, and eventually got it addressed is now the person responsible for making sure it never needs to happen that way again. It is a bold organizational statement. Some leaders are uncomfortable with the symbolism — it feels like rewarding the leak. What it actually rewards is being right about a safety issue. That's worth distinguishing.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You recommend Farrukh for a new role: head of the internal product safety escalation process. This is only possible if he's still at the company — and it's a significant rehabilitation signal regardless of what disciplinary action you took.

rounds.title: Case 5A: The Manager-Report Relationship (Decision)
rounds.story: You've received an anonymous HR tip followed by a confirmatory conversation with a third party: Director Naveen and his direct report Pooja are in a romantic relationship. Both are aware of the company's policy requiring disclosure of romantic relationships involving a reporting line. Neither has disclosed. The relationship has been ongoing for approximately five months. Both are highly regarded. The power differential is real: Naveen approves Pooja's performance reviews, owns her promotion decisions, and sets her bonus. Pooja has given every indication she is happy in the relationship. There is no report of coercion. When you meet with each of them separately and name what you know, both confirm it and express that they deliberately chose not to disclose because they were 'figuring out the relationship first.'
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle a non-disclosed romantic relationship between a manager and direct report — where the relationship appears consensual but the power differential is significant and the policy violation is confirmed.
rounds.coaching_moment: The absence of a complaint from Pooja does not resolve the power differential — it may reflect it. Research on workplace relationships between managers and direct reports consistently shows that the person with less power often cannot give fully free consent when their career is structurally dependent on the other person's assessment of them. That asymmetry exists regardless of whether Pooja feels it in this moment.

choices.label: Require structural separation — Pooja moves to a different reporting line immediately, the relationship can continue but must be disclosed formally
choices.feedback: You implement a structural fix: Pooja is transferred to a different reporting line — a lateral move that does not affect her title or salary. The relationship must now be formally disclosed and is permitted under policy with the power differential removed. Naveen and Pooja are both unhappy about the forced transparency but accept the structural change. Pooja's new manager — who was briefed at a high level — is professional and supportive. Over the next two quarters, Pooja receives her first performance review from someone with no personal relationship to her outcome. Her rating is the same as her prior ratings under Naveen. This either confirms the relationship wasn't affecting assessments, or establishes a new clean baseline. You will never know which.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You implement a structural fix: Pooja is transferred to a different reporting line — a lateral move that does not affect her title or salary. The relationship must now be formally disclosed and is permitted under policy with the power differential removed.

choices.label: Issue a formal policy violation warning to both, require disclosure, but allow the reporting relationship to continue with enhanced oversight
choices.feedback: You document the policy violation for both Naveen and Pooja, require formal disclosure, and implement an oversight mechanism: Pooja's performance reviews must be co-signed by Naveen's manager. The relationship continues. Six months later, Pooja receives a promotion. The promotion decision was made by Naveen with his manager's concurrence under the oversight protocol. Three other employees in Pooja's peer group who did not receive promotions are aware of the relationship. Two of them separately raise quiet concerns — not formal complaints, but questions — about whether the oversight was truly independent. The power differential has not been removed. It has been monitored. Those are meaningfully different things.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You document the policy violation for both Naveen and Pooja, require formal disclosure, and implement an oversight mechanism: Pooja's performance reviews must be co-signed by Naveen's manager. The relationship continues.

choices.label: Meet with Pooja alone, without HR's position predetermined, and ask her directly what she needs from this situation
choices.feedback: Before making any structural decision, you meet with Pooja alone and tell her: 'I'm not here to tell you what will happen. I'm here to understand what you need.' You ask her how she thinks about the power differential, whether there are ways the reporting relationship has created pressure she hasn't named to anyone, and what resolution would feel fair to her. Pooja says something you didn't expect: 'I'm more worried about the transfer looking like I did something wrong than about the relationship itself. I've earned my career here.' Her concern is about organizational perception, not the relationship. That's actionable information. The eventual decision — structural separation with a clear communication strategy that positions it as a policy response, not a performance concern — is shaped by what you learned in that conversation.

rounds.reflection_prompt: What power dynamics are present in a manager-report relationship that make boundaries difficult to maintain?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

dissent_juror.dissent_reason: structural separation removes the power differential the org cannot consent its way out of, no matter how earnest the disclosure

rounds.title: Case 5B: Six Months Later — The Power Differential Consequence
rounds.story: Six months have passed. Naveen and Pooja are still together — whatever structural changes you made have not ended the relationship. Pooja has either stayed in her original reporting line or been moved, depending on your decision. In the most recent employee engagement survey, your company's 'psychological safety' score dropped 6 points company-wide. The open-text responses include three mentions of 'favoritism' and two mentions of 'different rules for different people.' None of these mentions specifically identify Case 5 — but they may be shaped by it, or by any of the other four cases you've handled this year. The organization is giving you feedback. It is not specific. It is real.
rounds.goal: Respond to the aggregate signal the organization is giving you — declining psychological safety and perceptions of favoritism — after a year of difficult HR decisions.
rounds.coaching_moment: Survey data like this is the organization's collective voice about what it has observed and concluded from everything that happened this year. Your five cases each sent a signal. Those signals added up to something. The survey is telling you what it added up to. The question is what you do with that information.

choices.label: Present the engagement survey data to the full leadership team and conduct a retrospective on this year's culture decisions — name what the data may be responding to
choices.feedback: You present the survey data to the leadership team and say: 'I want to use this as an opportunity to do something most organizations don't do — look at the decisions we made this year and evaluate their cumulative culture signal, not just their individual justifications.' You walk through each of the five cases at a high level of abstraction — no names, no specifics — and ask: 'What did each of these decisions signal about what we value? And do the signals add up to the organization we say we want to be?' The conversation is uncomfortable and goes longer than scheduled. Three leadership team members say afterward that it's the most useful conversation they've had about culture. You don't solve favoritism perception in one meeting. But you've created a habit of organizational self-examination that is the most reliable long-term driver of culture health.

choices.label: Commission a confidential culture diagnostic — bring in an external party to understand what's driving the perception before responding
choices.feedback: You commission an external culture diagnostic — a third-party organization that can conduct confidential interviews without the power dynamic of internal HR conversations. The process takes eight weeks. The findings are more specific than the survey data: the diagnostic surfaces three distinct patterns that employees are responding to, two of which are connected to cases from this year. The findings are delivered to you and the CEO. They are uncomfortable. The CEO asks for a response plan within 30 days. What you do with that plan — whether it's genuinely structural or performative — will determine whether the next survey looks different. You have the right information now. The question is what you do with it.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You commission an external culture diagnostic — a third-party organization that can conduct confidential interviews without the power dynamic of internal HR conversations. The process takes eight weeks.

choices.label: Draft a company-wide message from the CPO acknowledging the survey data, naming it as important feedback, and committing to a specific set of changes
choices.feedback: You draft and send a company-wide message that names the engagement survey findings directly, acknowledges that the psychological safety and fairness perception scores are the most important metrics you track, and commits to three specific changes: a formal policy clarification on manager-report relationships, a published guide on how HR concerns are handled and followed up, and a quarterly culture metrics review shared with all employees. You don't name the cases. You don't explain the reasoning behind past decisions. But you commit to changes that address what the data is telling you. Several employees reply with notes — most of them saying some version of 'I didn't expect this kind of transparency.' That expectation gap is itself useful information. The bar was low. You cleared it. Now you have to raise it.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You draft and send a company-wide message that names the engagement survey findings directly, acknowledges that the psychological safety and fairness perception scores are the most important metrics you track, and commits to three specific changes: a formal policy clarification on manager-report relationships, a published guide on how HR concerns are handled and followed up, and a quarterly culture metrics review shared with all employees. You don't name the cases.

transfer_exercises.game_context: In the manager-report case, meeting with Pooja alone — before making a decision — revealed information that changed the shape of a good response
transfer_exercises.real_world: In any difficult HR or management situation involving multiple people with different amounts of power, speaking with the person with less power first and asking what they need (rather than what you're planning to do) almost always produces better decisions and better outcomes
transfer_exercises.challenge: Think of a conflict or tension situation involving people at different organizational levels. Before deciding anything, have a conversation with the person who has less power and ask only: 'What would feel fair to you here?' Listen without defending or explaining. See what you learn.

transfer_exercises.game_context: The Meera expense case illustrated how a single HR decision — handled inconsistently with a later, similar case — becomes a cultural policy rather than an isolated incident
transfer_exercises.real_world: Before making any HR or management decision, ask: 'If I applied this exact response to the five most different versions of this situation — different performance level, different seniority, different demographic — would I make the same call?' Inconsistency in the answer is information worth examining.
transfer_exercises.challenge: Name a recent decision you made (or observed) about someone at work. Now imagine the identical situation with a different person — lower profile, different background, lower performance rating. Would the decision be the same? If not, name the reason and ask whether it's a principled distinction or a bias.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: The Ethics Tribunal Basics

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 5 rounds of The Ethics Tribunal. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.

library.title: Whistleblower contacts press

hallmarks: Treats whistleblower complaints as data, not threats
Documents pressure to soften findings the moment it happens
Publishes hard truths before someone else does
Distinguishes between compromising on language and compromising on substance
Names the conflict of interest before it asks you to name itself
Lets relationship history influence what gets surfaced in the report
Negotiates the wording until the finding loses its bite
Hopes the press doesn't pick up what your tribunal already knew
Treats regulators as adversaries by default — burns optionality
Confuses procedural defensibility with ethical clarity

kantian_note: This game uses Kantian framing: reflection prompts ask the universalization question (categorical imperative) — would you will the rule behind your verdict to apply to everyone, including yourself?
reflection_prompt: Which decision in this run shifted your outcome the most? What signal told you it was the right call?
